title: Dogen's just sitting
hookLine: a cushion, a wall, and no technique at all: Zen's sitting practice
carry: practice and awakening are not two

cards: A round cushion on the floor. A plain wall a few feet away. Someone sits down, crosses their legs, rests their hands in their lap, and then nothing else happens.
No counting the breath. No phrase to repeat. No candle, no picture to hold in the mind.
A person just sits there, awake. That can sound like waiting for the real thing to start.
In one Zen school, this is the real thing, and the Japanese teacher Dogen gave it a name almost too plain to be a teaching: just sitting.

teach.b: Back on day one hundred three, the word zen turned out to mean meditation. Zazen is Zen's word for seated meditation, and Dogen's name for the way he taught it was shikantaza, usually put into English as just sitting.
First, it has no technique. The last block met practices with a job to do: count the breath, note the thought, scan the body. Just sitting sets the jobs down.
Second, the body does the work.

teach.h: BACK UPRIGHT, EYES OPEN, BREATH QUIET.
teach.b: In his short guide to zazen, Dogen's instructions are physical and plain: sit on a cushion, cross the legs, fold the hands, keep the back upright, don't lean left or right, forward or back. Eyes stay open, resting gently.
Breath goes quietly through the nose. Third, thoughts. They will come.
Dogen doesn't say to fight them or to follow them.

teach.h: A THOUGHT COMES: NOTICE, AND IT GOES.
teach.b: His advice, in paraphrase: when a thought arises, notice it, and in the noticing it goes. He passes on an old exchange, too: asked what you think about while sitting, a teacher answers, roughly, think of not-thinking.
And how do you do that? Non-thinking. It's meant to puzzle a little.

teach.h: NOT A TOOL. THE SITTING ITSELF.
teach.b: Fourth, the surprise: for Dogen, sitting isn't a tool for getting enlightenment later. He taught that practice and awakening aren't two separate things; the sitting is already what it's looking for.
Hard to hold in your head, which may be why he kept handing people a cushion instead of an argument. The Soto school, which traces itself to Dogen, puts just sitting at its heart.
Rinzai Zen also sits zazen, and often adds something else to the cushion. That's tomorrow.

how: In Soto Zen, practitioners sit zazen as shikantaza, upright with eyes open and no object of focus, often in a meditation hall together and at set times of day.

games.q: you're sitting zazen and a thought about tomorrow's meeting shows up. going by Dogen's advice, what do you do?
o: push it away hard and clear your mind.
notice it, and come back to sitting.
follow it and plan the meeting properly.
games.why: Dogen's advice, in paraphrase: when a thought arises, notice it, and in the noticing it goes. no fight, no chase.

practice: On a chair is fine: feet on the floor, back upright but not stiff, hands in your lap, eyes open and resting softly on the floor a little ahead.
Breathe through your nose and leave the breath alone; when a thought shows up, notice it, and come back to sitting. There's nothing to get right, and another day, ten minutes is a good next step.

wordCard.voice: Zazen. Seated meditation in Zen. In Dogen's way of teaching it, just sitting, with nothing added. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: the word Zen uses for seated meditation.

carryVoice: Your line: practice and awakening are not two. That's Dogen's just sitting: nothing added to it, and nothing missing from it. Until tomorrow.
